The wet weight attained by individuals at this same 300-day interval reaches 17500.0 grams , reflecting a substantial accumulation of somatic tissue during the post-metamorphic juvenile phase at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This mass gain is consistent with the energetic demands of a pelagic existence, where swift increases in body dimensions enhance both predatory capability and escape from larger nektonic hunters.

The onset of sexual maturation in Thysanoteuthis rhombus is marked by a mantle length at puberty of approximately 60.0 centimeters [Lp = approximately 60.0 centimeters], though notable sexual dimorphism exists in this trait. Males typically attain puberty between 40 and 55 centimeters in mantle length, whereas females require a more extended somatic investment, reaching reproductive activation at mantle lengths ranging from 55 to 65 centimeters. This divergence in pubertal size likely reflects the greater reproductive burden borne by females, which must allocate substantial resources toward the production of large, energy-rich egg masses. The transition from an immature post-metamorphic state to a reproductively active adult therefore represents a critical life-history bottleneck, imposing a minimum body size threshold that significantly influences population-level reproductive output.

Upon reaching terminal body size, diamond squid exhibit a maximum mantle length at death of 100.0 centimeters [Li = 100.0 centimeters], a dimension that places them among the larger members of the family Ommastrephidae. The corresponding wet weight at death has been recorded at 30000.0 grams [Wwi = 30000.0 grams], representing the culmination of a growth phase characterized by sustained anabolic investment. At the opposite end of the size spectrum, hatchlings emerge from eggs measuring approximately 3 millimeters in diameter, yielding a wet weight at birth of only 0.0141 grams [Wwb = 0.0141 grams]. This extraordinary range in body mass — spanning over six orders of magnitude from neonate to senescent adult — underscores the profound ontogenetic shift in trophic ecology and metabolic demand that defines the species’ life history.

Reproductive output in female diamond squid is substantial, with a cumulative reproductive investment at death of 480000.0 eggs  under a thermal regime of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This extraordinary fecundity is partitioned into discrete egg masses, each containing up to 43800 eggs, which are deposited as large, neutrally buoyant gelatinous ribbons that drift in warm surface waters. The production of such a large number of offspring is characteristic of a pelagic spawner employing a brood strategy that maximizes propagule dispersal at the cost of minimal maternal investment per individual zygote. Field surveys and laboratory observations indicate that females deposit these egg masses repeatedly throughout their reproductive lifespan, sustaining a high reproductive output that compensates for elevated early-life mortality among planktonic paralarvae.

Female diamond squid maintained at 15 °C [T = 15 °C] exhibit a maximum lifespan of 365.0 days [am = 365.0 days], a relatively short duration for a cephalopod of this body size. This compressed lifespan, common among oceanic oegopsids, is characterized by rapid somatic growth followed by a single, intense reproductive episode that precedes senescence and post-reproductive mortality. Members of the family Ommastrephidae similarly display semelparous life histories, with males often exhibiting slightly shorter lifespans. The synchronization of such a brief life with remarkably high fecundity — yielding a cumulative egg count that dwarfs that of many longer-lived molluscs — positions Thysanoteuthis rhombus as an exemplar of a fast-lived, high-output life-history strategy among cephalopods.
